These two variants provide different approaches for integrating multiple backbone models and transformer layers within the ensemble model, enabling the model to leverage diverse features and capture complex patterns in the input data.

The proposed IEViT (Iterative Expansion Vision Transformer) model is an extension of the ViT (Vision Transformer) architecture, incorporating concepts inspired by the ResNet (Residual Network). It introduces an iterative process in which the original input image is iteratively added to the output of each Transformer encoder layer. To facilitate this, a convolutional block is designed in parallel with the ViT network. The CNN block processes the entire input image and generates an embedding of the image denoted as ximg. This embedding is then concatenated to the output of each Transformer encoder layer, denoted as zl, thereby incorporating the complete image information throughout the encoding process.

The IEViT architecture comprises stacked 2D convolutional layers, followed by a 1D global maximum pooling layer within the CNN block. The resulting tensor is a feature embedding, ximg of dimension D. Additionally, the image is divided into N = H·W

P 2 patches, which are flattened to patches xp of size N × (P 2 · C). Subsequently, the patch embeddings zl are created by mapping the patches to D dimensions using 2D convolution layers. Position embeddings denoted as Epos, Epos ∈R(N+1)×D, are introduced to encode the positional information of each patch in the original image.

Firstly, the initial patch embedding zp and the positional encodings Epos are element-wise added. An optional class token might also be concatenated with zp.

z0 = zp + Epos (7)

where z0 represents the combined embeddings. The core iterative expansion process in IEViT occurs during the transformation of image embeddings through stacked Transformer encoder layers. At each layer l, the image embedding, ximg, is fused with the encoder output, zl, resulting in a combined representation denoted as zˆl. This process is mathematically represented as:

ˆl ∈R(N+1+l)×D. (8)

The iterative expansion in IEViT enhances its capability to capture spatial information and maintain global context, contributing to superior performance across diverse computer vision tasks.

We propose two novel variants to enhance the patch extraction step in IEViT, leveraging domain knowledge of the 20 diseases targeted for classification [16]. These variants address the importance of prioritizing patches from near the center of the image, where crucial features are expected to be prominent for the specific disease labels we’re targeting.

Variant 1- Unequal Patches: In this variant, we manually set the patch dimensions to be extracted from the image for forming the patch of embedding of dimension D. We extract patches with decreasing dimensions as we move closer to the center. This approach allocates more space to patches near the center, where crucial features are expected to be prominent. The patch dimensions, manually defined as 32x32, 16x16, and 8x8, progressively decrease towards the center.

Variant 2- Dynamic Patch Decomposer (DPD): This approach utilizes normalized learnable parameter importance weights for the initial 144 patches, each with a dimension of 32 × 32. The method dynamically determines which patches to subdivide based on their importance, using the formula for the new patch dimension (NPD):

NPD = 32 ×

wavg

where wi represents the weight of the i-th patch, wavg is the average weight, and k is a hyperparameter. Patches with NPD > 32 remain unchanged, while others are subdivided into dimensions NPD ×NPD after rounding NPD to the nearest factor of 32. The new patches are extracted, and their embedding zn is appended to the former patch embedding tensor zl at the position of the original patches that were divided or merged, as represented by the equation:

l = zl ⊕zn

A similar adjustment is applied to maintain positional encoding and adapt it for subdivided or merged patches. Specifically, the positional encoding is extended to accommodate new patches while preserving the existing ones, ensuring that spatial information is accurately represented throughout the encoding process. The positional encoding for the new patches is inserted at the position of the original patch in the encoding tensor. This extension is expressed by:

pos = Epos ⊕Enew

Additionally, the MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) head parameters are dynamically adjusted to handle the input changes due to patch subdivision and merging. Parameter sharing is employed to efficiently accommodate the new patches without a significant increase in model parameters, ensuring that the MLP weight matrix adapts to the varying input dimensions. Weight splicing is used when the patches are merged. This adaptive approach enhances the model’s ability to capture and utilize original and subdivided patch information.

In this subsection, we present two variants of the CTran model that incorporate the Iterative expansion concept from IEViT.

IECTe- Iterative Expansion C-Tran Ensembler: The IECTe variant combines ensemble model variant 2 with the IE concept by appending the reduced feature embeddings from the two CNN backbones x and y to each output of transformer layers. Concatenating feature embeddings along the num classes dimension (dim = 0):

z0 = [x, y]

ˆl = [zl, z0]

By incorporating these additional feature embeddings, the model gains a holistic understanding of the input image from multiple perspectives. This enables the model to leverage the strengths of both ResNet201 and DenseNet201 architectures, leading to enhanced representation learning and improved performance. The iterative nature of the IEViT approach ensures that the network retains knowledge of the entire input image throughout the Transformer encoding process. By iteratively concatenating the feature embeddings to the Transformer output, the IECTe model continuously ”remembers” the full image information, facilitating effective information fusion and promoting robust representations.

IeECT: Iterative Ensemble Expansion C-Tran- The IeECT variant focuses on reducing the overall model complexity for IECTe. In this variant, the feature embedding from DenseNet201 serves as the primary input to the Transformer (z0 = x), while the feature embedding from ResNet152 is appended to the Transformer output after each layer.

ˆl = [zl, y]

By employing this design, the IeECT model benefits from the expressive power of DenseNet201, which captures intricate image details and relationships. Simultaneously, the inclusion of the ResNet152 feature embedding allows the model to incorporate information from a different architectural perspective, enriching the representations with complementary insights. Using the IEViT concept in IeECT ensures that the model retains knowledge of the original image throughout the encoding process while maintaining fewer parameters. [1]

To evaluate the performance of our models, we used the same metrics as used in [15] for comparison on the same dataset. These metrics include F1-score, AUC, and mAP. ML mAP, ML F1, and ML AUC are calculated by averaging scores for each label, excluding the ”NORMAL” label- having the AUC and F1-score represented by Bin AUC and Bin F1 metric.

ML Score = ML mAP + ML AUC

The Model Score metric evaluates the overall performance by considering both disease classification and normalcy detection.

Model Score = ML Score + Bin AUC

The results of our experiments are presented in Table 6. As expected, the deeper DenseNet201 model surpassed the baseline C-Tran model that used DenseNet161. The ensemble models with deeper CNN backbones also demonstrated improved scores. The Strong Densenet and Weak Resnet ensemble variant 1, in particular, consistently achieved a model score above 0.91, surpassing the rest. It surpassed the baseline in 5 out of 8 metrics, scoring AUC less than 0.9 only in 1 label compared to 2 of the baseline. Fig. 3 shows its ROC curve. As seen in Table 6, this model also surpassed the state-of-the-art (SOTA) model, which had a score of 0.9. As for the ViT-based models, all of its variants showed superior performance compared to the C-Tran baseline model while maintaining lower computational complexity. Notably, the IEViT v2 DPD variant displayed slightly better performance among the IEViT models for 32 × 32 dimension patch. The IE variants

of C-Tran also exhibited slight improvements over the baseline, showcasing that the IE concept can be advantageous even in generic transformer architectures while maintaining lower complexity.

In summary, our research underscores the effectiveness of hybrid models in classifying retinal images despite the limitations of a small, imbalanced dataset. While we have made commendable progress in multi-label retinal disease classification, we acknowledge the constraints imposed by data size and class imbalances, which could lead to randomness and potential overfitting.

Despite these challenges, our work represents a significant step in advancing deep learning-based strategies for accurate retinal disease classification. It also opens avenues for further refinement. We plan to focus on improving model interpretability to address these limitations and enhance practical utility. In our future work, we aim to explore the integration of Shapley values to unravel the causal relationships behind our model’s predictions, making them more transparent and understandable.

In conclusion, our study highlights the potential of combining transformers and ensemble learning to tackle retinal disease classification challenges. Through our ongoing efforts to enhance interpretability and delve into advanced techniques, we aim to pave the way for more robust, interpretable, and effective models that can significantly benefit the field of medical diagnostics.

sources.title: Retinal Fundus Multi-Disease Image Classification using Hybrid CNN-Transformer-Ensemble Architectures
sources.text: Abstract. Our research is motivated by the urgent global issue of a large population affected by retinal diseases, which are evenly distributed but underserved by specialized medical expertise, particularly in non-urban areas. Our primary objective is to bridge this healthcare gap by developing a comprehensive diagnostic system capable of accurately predicting retinal diseases solely from fundus images. However, we faced significant challenges due to limited, diverse datasets and imbalanced class distributions. To overcome these issues, we have devised innovative strategies.

Additionally, the MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) head parameters are dynamically adjusted to handle the input changes due to patch subdivision and merging. sources.text: The proposed IEViT (Iterative Expansion Vision Transformer) model is an extension of the ViT (Vision Transformer) architecture, incorporating concepts inspired by the ResNet (Residual Network). It introduces an iterative process in which the original input image is iteratively added to the output of each Transformer encoder layer. To facilitate this, a convolutional block is designed in parallel with the ViT network. The CNN block processes the entire input image and generates an embedding of the image denoted as ximg. This embedding is then concatenated to the output of each Transformer encoder layer, denoted as zl, thereby incorporating the complete image information throughout the encoding process.

The Strong Densenet and Weak Resnet ensemble variant 1, in particular, consistently achieved a model score above 0.91, surpassing the rest. sources.title: Retinal Fundus Multi-Disease Image Classification using Hybrid CNN-Transformer-Ensemble Architectures
sources.text: Abstract. Our research is motivated by the urgent global issue of a large population affected by retinal diseases, which are evenly distributed but underserved by specialized medical expertise, particularly in non-urban areas. Our primary objective is to bridge this healthcare gap by developing a comprehensive diagnostic system capable of accurately predicting retinal diseases solely from fundus images. However, we faced significant challenges due to limited, diverse datasets and imbalanced class distributions. To overcome these issues, we have devised innovative strategies.

document.title: Towards Reducing Food Waste: A High-Accuracy Hybrid Model for Fruit Freshness Prediction via CNN and Metadata

pages.text:
Towards Reducing Food Waste: A High-Accuracy

Hybrid Model for Fruit Freshness Prediction via

CNN and Metadata

Md Asif Uddin

Dept of Computer Science and Engineering

BRAC University Dhaka, Bangladesh md.asif.uddin@g.bracu.ac.bd

Abstract—Food waste continues to be a major global issue, with a significant portion of edible food discarded prematurely due to inaccurate spoilage predictions. In industries such as retail, the food supply chain, and households, fruits, vegetables, and packaged goods often go to waste because of poor management and inaccurate expiration forecasts. The lack of real-time monitoring and efficient prediction methods contributes to economic losses and environmental harm. This study aims to tackle this issue by developing an AI-driven solution that predicts the expiry dates of food items using both image data and environmental metadata, including temperature, humidity, and days since purchase. By employing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image analysis and integrating Machine Learning models like Random Forest and MLP, the system can predict the freshness of food with high accuracy. The tool will assist retailers, food suppliers, and consumers in reducing food waste, optimizing decision-making, and promoting sustainable food management practice

Index Terms—Food Expiry, Machine Learning, Convolutional Neural Networks, Random Forest, MLP, Image Analysis, Sustainability

Food waste is a significant global issue, impacting the environment, economy, and food security. A large portion of edible food is discarded prematurely, particularly in retail, the food supply chain, and households, due to inaccurate spoilage predictions. This issue arises from the lack of real-time monitoring and unreliable expiration forecasting methods, which lead to economic losses and environmental harm, especially in industries dealing with perishable goods like fruits and vegetables. This research seeks to address the problem by developing an AI-powered solution that predicts food expiration using both image data and environmental metadata such as temperature, humidity, and days since purchase. By leveraging Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image analysis and combining them with models like Random Forest and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), the system aims to accurately classify food as fresh or spoiled. The goal is to provide a realtime tool that helps retailers, food suppliers, and consumers make informed decisions, reducing food waste and promoting sustainable food management practices

Puja Banik

Dept of Computer Science and Engineering

BRAC University Dhaka, Bangladesh puja.banik@g.bracu.ac.bd

Fig. 1. Fresh vs Rotten Food Samples

Food waste is a significant global problem, and effectively predicting food expiry is a key solution to reduce waste. Recent studies have explored the use of machine learning, particularly deep learning, to predict the freshness and shelf life of food products. ”Artificial Intelligence for Shelf-Life Prediction” (2025) by Xie et al. [4] explores AI models that use image data and environmental factors such as temperature and humidity to predict the expiry of food. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are applied to increase accuracy in freshness predictions, emphasizing the potential of AI in reducing food waste by providing more accurate expiry dates. Similarly, ”Predicting Shelf-Life of Fruits” (2024) by Liu et al. [2] combines CNN for image classification with environmental data like temperature and storage duration to predict fruit freshness. This hybrid approach, leveraging both image and environmental factors, significantly improves accuracy in predicting ripeness and reduces spoilage, especially in retail environments. Further, Zhang et al.’s ”Freshness Monitoring in Supply Chains” (2025) [6] develops a system that combines CNN-based image processing with environmental metadata to monitor food freshness in real time throughout the supply chain. This system enhances food safety and reduces waste in transportation and storage. ”Privacy-Preserving Ordinal-Meta Learning for Food Freshness” (2025) by Kumar et al. [7] introduces an innovative privacy-preserving approach using ordinal meta-learning techniques for predicting food freshness. This method categorizes freshness levels for more granular predic-

Shahrin Farah Tasnim

Dept of Computer Science and Engineering

BRAC University Dhaka, Bangladesh shahrin.farah.tasnim@g.bracu.ac.bd

tions, which could be valuable for consumer-facing freshness prediction systems, ensuring privacy while maintaining prediction accuracy. Similarly, ”Deep Learning-Based Classification of Rotten Fruits” (2025) by Huang et al. [8] applies CNNs to classify fresh and rotten fruits, highlighting the promise of deep learning in automating spoilage detection and reducing food waste. ”Predicting Shelf-Life of Fruits: A Multifactorial Approach” (2025) by Wang et al. [5] combines image-based freshness detection with environmental metadata, improving model accuracy with the integration of storage temperature and time. Despite the high computational costs, this approach offers significant potential for practical use in retail to limit food waste. Li et al.’s ”Intelligent Monitoring of Fruit and Vegetable Freshness in Supply Chains” (2025) focuses on realtime freshness monitoring by combining image analysis with supply chain metadata, enabling continuous freshness evaluation to maintain food quality and minimize waste. Zhao et al.’s ”Fruit Freshness Prediction Using Transfer Learning” (2025) employs transfer learning with the ResNet-18 model, trained on over 55,000 images, to predict the freshness of fruits across different types and storage conditions. This scalable approach enhances model generalization and efficiency. Lastly, ”Canned Apple Freshness Detection Using Hybrid Approach” (2025) by Guo et al. [1] proposes using CNNs to extract features from canned apples, followed by machine learning algorithms for classification. Despite challenges with processing time, this model demonstrates the potential of image recognition and machine learning in evaluating food freshness, particularly in the canned goods industry where waste reduction is crucial.

The dataset includes 13,599 fruit images (10,901 for training, 2,698 for testing), categorized as apples, bananas, and oranges, and labeled as ”fresh” or ”rotten.” The training set is balanced with 6,161 rotten and 4,740 fresh fruits, and similar distribution is maintained in the test set. Image dimensions range from 144x116 to 860x518 pixels, with an average brightness of 165.88. Additional features include texture scores, storage temperature (5°C to 30°C), humidity (40% to 90%), and days since purchase (0 to 12 days). This comprehensive dataset ensures effective model evaluation and generalization.

Fig. 2. Missing Values (Train Data)

In this study, data preprocessing is essential to ensure the dataset is ready for modeling. Initially, label encoding is applied to the “Fruit” and “Freshness” columns to transform the categorical variables into numerical values, which are required for machine learning models. The “Fruit” column is encoded using a label encoder, and the “Freshness” column is also encoded to create target labels.

Fig. 3. Correlation Heatmap (Numeric Features))

The next step involves splitting the dataset into features (X) and the target variable (y), using columns such as “fruit enc”, “days since purchase”, “storage temperature (°C)”, “humidity percentage”, and “handle level (0-100)” as features.

Additionally, the dataset is standardized using a standard scaler to ensure that the features have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. This improves the performance of machine learning algorithms by making the learning process more efficient.

The study applies multiple machine learning algorithms to classify fresh fruitness with Random Forest multilayer, Perceptron MLP, and convolutional neural network CNN Bing the primary models. The Random Forest model is used due to its ability to handle large data sets and its robustness against overfitting. The MLP is implemented using a pipeline for scalable processing and CNN is applied for image classification. Each model is evaluated using accuracy, precision recall and F1 score matrices, as well as through evaluations such as ROC curves and confusion matrices. The models are implemented using Python in the following libraries: scikit-learn for preprocessing, model training and evolution, pandas for data manipulation, matplotlib and Seabourn for visualization and thoughts for deep learning models. The primary tools used include LevelEncoder for encoding categorical data, Standard- Scalar for future scaling and machine learning algorithms like random forest, MLP and CNN for classification. Evolution metrics like accuracy classification report and ROC curves are utilised for performance assessment. The data set is processed using pandas library, With models being trained and tested using the sklearn and torch libraries.

• a) Convolutional Neural Network (CNN): CNN outperformed all other models, achieving an accuracy of

96%. CNN led in precision, recall, and F1-score for both the “fresh” and “rotten” classes, showcasing its exceptional ability to classify both classes correctly. CNN’s performance was also reflected in its AUC of 0.995 and Average Precision of 0.994, indicating its superior ability to distinguish between classes and accurately predict freshness.

• b) Support Vector Machine (SVM ): SVM performed well, especially in precision for the ”fresh” class, achieving an accuracy of 0.799. Although it did not surpass CNN, it was competitive in terms of classification performance, with a balanced precision-recall performance across both classes. The AUC for SVM was 0.897, and it achieved an Average Precision of 0.932.

• c) Gradient Boosting:Gradient Boosting performed closely to Random Forest, with an accuracy of 0.811. It was strong in distinguishing between the ”rotten” class with high precision. The AUC score of 0.915 further indicated its effectiveness, and its Average Precision of 0.942 confirmed its strength in predicting freshness and spoilage.

• d) Multilayer Perceptron (MLP):MLP showed a similar pattern to Gradient Boosting, achieving an accuracy of 0.78. While its precision and recall were competitive for both classes, the model performed slightly lower in terms of AUC (0.903) and lacked the precision-recall edge of CNN, with no Average Precision value provided.

• e) Random Forest:Random Forest performed competitively with an accuracy of 0.81, similar to Gradient Boosting. It excelled in precision for the ”rotten” class, though its recall for ”fresh” was lower. The AUC of 0.914 demonstrated its strong ability to classify correctly, and its Average Precision was 0.85, reflecting solid performance overall.

In this section, we will discuss the results of our models and the challenges encountered during the project. The performance comparison of five machine learning models—CNN, SVM, Gradient Boosting, MLP, and Random Forest—reveals that CNN outperforms all other models in terms of accuracy, achieving 96%. CNN leads in precision, recall, and F1-score for both the “fresh” and “rotten” classes, highlighting its superior ability to classify both classes correctly. Random Forest shows competitive performance with an accuracy of 81%, while MLP and Gradient Boosting provide similar results, with accuracy scores of 78% and 81%, respectively. SVM, though slightly behind, performs well, particularly in precision for the “fresh” class. The ROC AUC scores indicate that CNN and Gradient Boosting are the strongest performers, with CNN achieving an outstanding AUC of 0.995. The precision-recall curves further emphasize CNN’s edge, showing the highest Average Precision (AP) of 0.994. These results suggest that CNN is the most effective model for this classification task due to its high precision, recall, and overall performance metrics.

The performance analysis of the five models—CNN, Random Forest, MLP, Gradient Boosting, and SVM—reveals distinct differences in their ability to classify fresh and rotten fruits. CNN achieves the highest accuracy at 96%, outperformance in precision, recall, and F1-score across both classes. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting also perform competitively, with Random Forest achieving an accuracy of 81%, and Gradient Boosting following closely. MLP and

SVM show relatively lower accuracy compared to CNN, with MLP achieving an accuracy of 78% and SVM at 80%. The AUC values show that CNN has the highest AUC at 0.995, indicating the model’s strong ability to distinguish between the classes.

Fig. 6. Metrics By Class

The CNN model’s success can be attributed to its deep architecture, which allows it to capture spatial features from images effectively, resulting in high precision and recall. The Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models, being ensemble methods, also show strong performance, especially in terms of precision for the ”rotten” class. However, their recall for the ”fresh” class is slightly lower. MLP, despite being a fully connected network, struggles with capturing complex patterns as effectively as CNN, leading to lower performance in both precision and recall. SVM, with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel, demonstrates solid performance in precision for the ”fresh” class but is less effective for ”rotten.”

One limitation of this study is that the models were only evaluated based on standard metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. While these metrics provide a comprehensive view of model performance, they do not account for real-time performance or model robustness under different conditions such as noise or varying data distributions. Additionally, the models were not tuned for hyperparameters, which may affect their performance in real-world applications.

Future improvements can focus on hyperparameter tuning for each model to optimize performance. For instance, applying techniques like grid search or random search for model selection can improve the models’ accuracy. Furthermore, increasing the size and diversity of the dataset or augmenting the current data with more examples could help enhance model robustness and generalization. Additionally, exploring other advanced models, such as deep learning techniques beyond CNNs (e.g., transformers), might provide a performance boost.

This study evaluated the performance of Gradient Boosting Classifier (GBC), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for classifying fruit freshness as “fresh” or “rotten”. The GBC model showed 81.1% accuracy, with high precision for “Fresh” (96.5%) and solid recall (69.3%). The SVM model performed well with 79.9% accuracy but did not outperform GBC or CNN. CNN excelled with the highest accuracy (96.4%) and superior ability

to classify both “Fresh” and “Rotten” fruits, as demonstrated by the confusion matrix and ROC curves.

Despite the strong results, there are areas for improvement. Models like Random Forest may suffer from overfitting, and CNNs require significant computational resources. Future work could focus on addressing class imbalances, using techniques like SMOTE, hyperparameter tuning, and integrating environmental features (e.g., temperature and humidity). sources.title: Towards Reducing Food Waste: A High-Accuracy Hybrid Model for Fruit Freshness Prediction via CNN and Metadata
sources.text: Abstract—Food waste continues to be a major global issue, with a significant portion of edible food discarded prematurely due to inaccurate spoilage predictions. In industries such as retail, the food supply chain, and households, fruits, vegetables, and packaged goods often go to waste because of poor management and inaccurate expiration forecasts. The lack of real-time monitoring and efficient prediction methods contributes to economic losses and environmental harm. This study aims to tackle this issue by developing an AI-driven solution that predicts the expiry dates of food items using both image data and environmental metadata, including temperature, humidity, and days since purchase.

The dataset includes 13,599 fruit images (10,901 for training, 2,698 for testing), categorized as apples, bananas, and oranges, and labeled as ”fresh” or ”rotten.” The training set is balanced with 6,161 rotten and 4,740 fresh fruits, and similar distribution is maintained in the test set. Image dimensions range from 144x116 to 860x518 pixels, with an average brightness of 165.88. Additional features include texture scores, storage temperature (5°C to 30°C), humidity (40% to 90%), and days since purchase (0 to 12 days). This comprehensive dataset ensures effective model evaluation and generalization.

sources.text: In this section, we will discuss the results of our models and the challenges encountered during the project. The performance comparison of five machine learning models—CNN, SVM, Gradient Boosting, MLP, and Random Forest—reveals that CNN outperforms all other models in terms of accuracy, achieving 96%. CNN leads in precision, recall, and F1-score for both the “fresh” and “rotten” classes, highlighting its superior ability to classify both classes correctly. Random Forest shows competitive performance with an accuracy of 81%, while MLP and Gradient Boosting provide similar results, with accuracy scores of 78% and 81%, respectively. SVM, though slightly behind, performs well, particularly in precision for the “fresh” class.

sources.title: Towards Reducing Food Waste: A High-Accuracy Hybrid Model for Fruit Freshness Prediction via CNN and Metadata
sources.text: The CNN model’s success can be attributed to its deep architecture, which allows it to capture spatial features from images effectively, resulting in high precision and recall. The Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models, being ensemble methods, also show strong performance, especially in terms of precision for the ”rotten” class. However, their recall for the ”fresh” class is slightly lower. MLP, despite being a fully connected network, struggles with capturing complex patterns as effectively as CNN, leading to lower performance in both precision and recall. SVM, with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel, demonstrates solid performance in precision for the ”fresh” class but is less effective for ”rotten.”

sources.text: Abstract—Food waste continues to be a major global issue, with a significant portion of edible food discarded prematurely due to inaccurate spoilage predictions. In industries such as retail, the food supply chain, and households, fruits, vegetables, and packaged goods often go to waste because of poor management and inaccurate expiration forecasts. The lack of real-time monitoring and efficient prediction methods contributes to economic losses and environmental harm. This study aims to tackle this issue by developing an AI-driven solution that predicts the expiry dates of food items using both image data and environmental metadata, including temperature, humidity, and days since purchase.

Our research is motivated by the urgent global issue of a large population affected by retinal diseases, which are evenly distributed but underserved by specialized medical expertise, particularly in non-urban areas. what limitations do the authors state ab.question: What limitations do the authors state about their own work?

sources.text: The proposed IEViT (Iterative Expansion Vision Transformer) model is an extension of the ViT (Vision Transformer) architecture, incorporating concepts inspired by the ResNet (Residual Network). how does celloracle simulate gene pertur.question: How does CellOracle simulate gene perturbation?
how does celloracle simulate gene pertur.answer: CellOracle simulates gene perturbation through a four-step process [2]. First, data preprocessing is conducted to prepare the input data. Second, signal propagation within the inferred GRN model is simulated, where the input TF perturbation is propagated side-by-side within the network model [6]. Third, the transition probabilities are estimated based on the GRN model [2]. Finally, the directionality of the future transition in cell identity is projected onto the dimensional reduction embedding [2]. The simulated gene expression shift vector is then used to project the directionality of the future transition in cell identity [2]. The simulated gene expression shift vector is used to represent the simulated initial gene expression shift after TF perturbation [3].

In silico gene perturbation using CellOracle

To gain mechanistic insight into the regulation of cell identity, we developed an in silico strategy to simulate changes in cell identity upon TF perturbation. CellOracle uses custom GRN modelling (Extended Data Fig. 1a) to simulate global downstream shifts in gene expression following knockout (KO) or overexpression of TFs. These simulated values are converted into a vector map of transitions in cell identity, which enables simulated changes in cell identity to be intuitively visualized within a low-dimension space (Fig. 1a and Methods). In silico perturbation involves four steps. (1) Cell-type- or cell-state-specific GRN configurations are constructed using cluster-wise regularized linear regression models with multi-omics data.

Simulation of cell identity following perturbation of regulatory genes The central purpose of CellOracle is to understand how a GRN governs cell identity. Toward this goal, we designed CellOracle to make use of inferred GRN configurations to simulate how cell identity changes following perturbation of regulatory genes. The simulated gene expression values are converted into 2D vectors representing the direction of cell-state transition, adapting the visualization method previously used by RNA velocity52. This process consists of four steps: (i) data preprocessing; (ii) signal propagation within the GRN; (iii) estimation of transition probabilities; and (iv) analysis of simulated transition in cell identity.

results.text:
The SCENIC algorithm integrates a tree-based GRN inference algorithm with information on TF binding7.

Preparation of input data for GRN inference We used the Tabula Muris scRNA-seq dataset for GRN construction input data56. Cells were subsampled for each tissue on the basis of the original tissue-type annotation: spleen, lung, muscle, liver and kidney. Data for each tissue were processed using the standard Seurat workflow, including data normalization, log transformation, finding variable features, scaling, principal component analysis (PCA) and Louvain clustering. The data were downsampled to 2,000 cells and 10,000 genes using highly variable genes detected by the corresponding Seurat function.

results.text: The study applies multiple machine learning algorithms to classify fresh fruitness with Random Forest multilayer, Perceptron MLP, and convolutional neural network CNN Bing the primary models. The Random Forest model is used due to its ability to handle large data sets and its robustness against overfitting. The MLP is implemented using a pipeline for scalable processing and CNN is applied for image classification. Each model is evaluated using accuracy, precision recall and F1 score matrices, as well as through evaluations such as ROC curves and confusion matrices.
